Accident Risk Assessor

A team project for CS 4641 (Machine Learning) at Georgia Tech, spring 2023. Five students tried to predict whether a crash happens, given a place, a time, and road, weather, driver and vehicle details. The data is the public crash reports of Montgomery County, Maryland.

The result

On the fair test, the random forest scored 67.7% accuracy, below the 75.0% of always answering "no crash". It was trained on 155,707 real crash records plus three times as many "random negatives": real crash records with the location, the time of day or the date swapped for another record's. Three of every four test rows are negatives, so a model that always says "no crash" scores 75.0%. The forest found 651 of the 31,141 real crashes (2%). No model in the project did better than that baseline on random negatives.

The 98% figure comes from a different set of negatives. The same random forest scored 98.2% when the negatives were built by hand: each feature drawn from a probability distribution meant to match the real data, with a few linked pairs such as vehicle make and model. Those rows are easy to tell apart from real records: 81.5% of them lie outside a latitude/longitude box that holds 96.2% of the real crashes. Location alone gives most of them away. So the 98% shows how well the model spots generated rows, not how well it predicts crashes.

The report flags both problems in its own words: the random-negative model "almost never correctly guesses accidents" (p. 3), and a model on the hand-built set "may be overfitting to the dataset due to how the non-accident samples were created" (p. 5).

Results

Each model trains on 80% of a dataset and is scored on the other 20% (the neural network: 67% and 33%). "Crashes found" is recall on the crash class. Report page numbers refer to CS-4641-Project-Report.pdf.

Notes on reading these numbers:

  • Three of every four rows are negatives, so accuracy near 75% can mean a model learned nothing. On random negatives, LightGBM answered "no crash" for every test row and XGBoost on PCA data for all but 10 (their confusion matrices show it). The neural network's 74.9% and 75.5% are close to the share of negatives in its two datasets (75.0% and 75.4%).
  • modelling/gbdt.py as committed trains XGBoost on 5 PCA components. The report does not say whether the 86.6% run used them.
  • The 81.5% and 96.2% figures above come from the two committed CSVs: the box spans the 1st to 99th percentile of the real crashes' latitude and longitude (38.965–39.275° N, 76.936–77.315° W). 3.8% of real crashes and 3.8% of random negatives lie outside it.

The data

  • Source: Montgomery County's Crash Reporting – Drivers Data. The report and one file name call the area "Baltimore". The records are Montgomery County's, next to Washington, D.C. Their median point is 39.08° N, 77.11° W. The location filter in data/Scripts/csv_cleaner.ipynb keeps 38.8–39.5° N and 76.8–77.7° W, which leaves Baltimore city outside.
  • Size: data/Prev Cleaning Stages/Original_Data.csv holds 155,811 rows and 43 columns. After the location filter and cleaning, 155,707 crash records remain (the report's introduction says 155,108).
  • Features: columns that describe the crash after it happened (collision type, severity, driver at fault and so on) were dropped. 24 columns remain in data/Accident Data/Column_Cleaned_Data.csv. The date and time became day of week, day of year, week of year, month, year and minute of the day.
  • PCA: data/Scripts/pca.py keeps the fewest components that hold 99% of the variance. On the crash records that is 5 (data/Accident Data/Accident_PCA_Data.csv). It centres the columns but does not scale them, so columns with large ranges dominate the components.

Pipeline, as committed (the notebook and pca.py write output.csv; the stage files were renamed by hand):

Original_Data.csv (155,811 rows) ──csv_cleaner.ipynb: location filter──► Baltimore_Area.csv (155,707 rows)
  ──csv_cleaner.ipynb: column clean-up──► Cleaned_Data.csv ──► Accident Data/Column_Cleaned_Data.csv (24 columns)
Numerical_Data.csv (categories as integer codes; the script that made it is not in the repo)
Numerical_Data + Column_Cleaned_Data ──combination_numerical_and_text.py──► normalized_numerical_data.csv (crashes)
normalized_numerical_data ──nonaccidentscript.py─────────► data/balanced_data.csv (random negatives, 3 per crash)
                          ──(generator not in the repo)──► data/balanced_nonrandom_data.csv (hand-built negatives)
                          ──pca.py───────────────────────► Accident_PCA_Data.csv (5 components)
data/Balanced_Data_PCA.csv: 5 PCA components of balanced_data.csv (data/New_PCA_Data.csv is an identical copy)

How to run

The CSV files (about 590 MB) are stored in Git LFS. Install Git LFS and run git lfs install before you clone; in a clone made without it, run git lfs pull to replace the pointer files.

The code was written in 2023 for Python 3 with TensorFlow 2. Install the packages:

pip install "pandas<2" numpy scikit-learn xgboost lightgbm tensorflow matplotlib

combination_numerical_and_text.py calls Series.dt.weekofyear, which pandas deprecated in 1.1, so use pandas 1.x.

Models (run from modelling/; each prints a confusion matrix and accuracy):

cd modelling
python randomforest.py     # reads ../data/balanced_nonrandom_data.csv; change it to balanced_data.csv for random negatives
python lgbm.py             # same input file as randomforest.py
python gbdt.py             # XGBoost on 5 PCA components, hand-built negatives
python neural-net.py       # random negatives, 3 epochs
python location-dbscan.py  # DBSCAN (eps 0.03, min 1000 points) on a 30% sample of crash locations; slow

With scikit-learn 1.2.2 and pandas 1.5.3, randomforest.py prints the same confusion matrices and accuracies as the committed screenshots: 0.9823650714641258 as committed, and 0.6772795144742546 with balanced_data.csv.

Data scripts: data/Scripts/pca.py runs from the repo root. combination_numerical_and_text.py and nonaccidentscript.py read and write bare file names, so run them inside data/Accident Data/ (the committed balanced_data.csv lives one level up, in data/). nonaccidentscript.py is slow: it checks each new row against every crash record. The plotting scripts in visualizations/ and csv_cleaner.ipynb read the raw data.gov download or paths on the authors' machines. Set FILE_PATH (or file_path) before running them.

Who built what

Five students built this project. The contribution table on page 8 of the report names each member and their part.

  • Saahil Sanganeriya built the random negatives with a teammate (data/Scripts/nonaccidentscript.py, data/balanced_data.csv), trained the random forest (modelling/randomforest.py) and ran the LightGBM comparison (modelling/lgbm.py). He also wrote the introduction and problem definition and took the data-cleaning tasks in the project timeline.
  • The other four members cleaned and formatted the data, built the hand-built negatives, ran PCA, trained XGBoost and the neural network, ran DBSCAN, made the project page (index.html, with _config.yml, layouts/ and assets/) and the presentation video, and wrote the final report.

Every commit in this repo is Saahil's because he uploaded the team's work here in September 2023.

Presentation video (uploaded by a teammate): https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FM7b4zGDyb0
